utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Prosecution has announced that it would have two preliminary matters to raise.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first is more of a housekeeping matter. That is that we received the revised English translation for P2838, which was 65 ter 28735. This document was used with Witness -- it was used on 22nd of September 2014. If we look at transcript page 25993, and T25990, the issue was that the text within the stamp was incomplete in the English translation. The revised translation has been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 01063030-ET. The Defence has indicated that they have no objection to the revised translation. We would request that the court officer be instructed to replace the current translation with the revised version and that the document be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document was admitted, isn't it? Yes. Then, Madam Registrar, you're instructed to replace the current translation with the revised one uploaded into e-court under number 01063030-ET. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Last week, the Chamber had asked the parties to provide an update as to 65 ter 1D02733, a collection of documents which the Defence had tendered as an associated exhibit to the evidence of Witness Djuric. Each request under the subject line each document in the collection identifies the name of a candidate. The Prosecution's demographics units has reviewed the names contained in those requests. The Prosecution was not able to verify the ethnicity of every name on the list. However, on the basis of our review, we do not contest that the large majority of the names appear to be Muslim. It is our position that some of the names appear to have been self-reported as Yugoslav or as another ethnicity in the census. When I say "another," I mean not Muslims, Serbs, or Croats. Separately, some names appear to have been misspelled in the list. The Prosecution has carefully reviewed those names. It is our position that it is most likely that one or more are Croats while the large majority are most likely to be Muslims, so -- and I -- in short, we aren't able to agree that all of them are Muslims. We are able to agree that the large majority appear to be Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. That's hereby on the record. And thank you for the update. Then could the -- Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want to inform Your Honours that there is a change in the schedule of the coming witnesses. One of our witnesses actually felt very bad. We had to return him home. So it's protected witnesses GRM 162 so the next witness after this one would be Mr. Sipovac, and then after him would be Mr. Veselinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that witness will be available in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That we were informed about the return. And -- thank you very much for informing us. And the Chamber appreciates that the Defence is so organised that we can hear then the testimony of the witness after the one who returned without further delays. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time for a few matters. The first deals with D686. The Chamber hereby puts on the record that document -- the document MFI'd as D686 bears 65 ter number 1D04059 and not 65 ter 1D04058, as was mentioned yesterday. And, therefore, the Registry, Madam Registrar, is instructed to replace 65 ter 1D04059 with 65 ter 1D04058a, which had been admitted into evidence yesterday as D686. Then another matter. It is about informing the Chamber about certain matters via e-mail. The Chamber advises the parties that every clarification or correction regarded tendered evidence has to be made on the record. Information submitted via e-mail will not be considered by the Chamber when evaluating the evidence. I have another item, but I leave that for a later moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Komad.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Ms. Bibles will now continue her cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And good morning, sir. I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like to start this morning by looking at D760. We're referring to D760 in paragraph 26. That's your Karadzic statement. Where you describe that with the breakout of clashes the Crisis Staffs were left to their own devices and in a large number of cases, Serbian authorities didn't have information about their work. And actually we could probably most efficiently go right to P3899, please. Sir, as this document comes up on the screen, you will see that it is an announcement from President Karadzic acting as president of the National Security Council on 4 April 1992. And if we can go to page 2 in the English - and obviously stay on this page in the B/C/S - and look at the last paragraph. We see Karadzic ordering Crisis Staffs to be activated and the Serbian armed forces to be raised anywhere where people respond to the mobilisation call of the Presidency. You see that, sir.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Let's look at some of the police response to this. If we could have P3193. And, sir, this is a report on the work of the Rogatica Crisis Staff from April to June 1992. And we see at the beginning that the Crisis Staff was established on 8 April 1992, some four days after the announcement that we just reviewed. So this is an example of a municipality implementing an order from central Bosnian Serb authorities; right?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question to me?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: The question was whether this is an example of a municipality level implementing an order from the central Bosnian Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an explicit answer to this question. All I can say is that the party policy and that of the political leadership was to act the way I described in my statement. Crisis Staffs were formed as needed at local levels. And as for the coincidence that the dates are close to each other, it's possible that there was such a suggestion, but the staffs were formed depending on the needs or on the crisis situations.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: All right. With respect to your statement and that has to do with paragraph 26 in your statement where you indicated that Serb authorities did not have information about the work of these Crisis Staffs, I'd like to move to page 5 in both versions of this particular document please. And I'd ask to you look I believe in the middle of the page in the original version where there's a paragraph that starts with: "Apart from numerous ..." Have you located that paragraph? "Apart from numerous oral and direct contacts ..." I'll go ahead and read it so that we have clarity: "Apart from numerous oral and direct" --

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found it, yes, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: "... the Crisis Staff also co-operated with many bodies in written form such as the Presidency of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the government, varies ministries of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the army, Serbian police, and some other bodies." So, sir, it's true that the Rogatica Crisis Staff was both responding to and communicating with the RS government, army, and police; right?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably the contacts existed where this was possible. I mentioned that the communications system was already impaired and communications were very difficult. As you know well, there were no mobile phones at that time, and phones and other ways of communication were proceeding with great difficulty. Probably there were contacts where it was possible. I really couldn't say. I wasn't able to be in each situation and know about all of these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Well, sir, the language of this paragraph is that, apart from numerous oral and direct contacts, the Rogatica Crisis Staff was obviously able to co-operate during this time-period with the relevant central Serbian authorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say. As I said before, Rogatica is some 60 kilometres away from Sarajevo, and probably because it was so close, it is possible that there were contacts. But I really couldn't say what the form of these contacts was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, it's clear that in the Crisis Staff's very own report, they reflect that they were able to both communicate and respond with the central authorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possible. If that's what the documents say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, sir, let's move now to actually a letter that you have drafted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 16943.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And this comes up on the screen, you'll see that it is a letter from you to various SAOs around Bosnia and Herzegovina, stating that Crisis Staffs are being abolished and being replaced with War Presidencies. Can you confirm that this is a letter that you sent out on 31st of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And this letter, in short, confirms that presidents of Crisis Staffs are to become War Commissioners; correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. They did not have to -- it didn't have to be the presidents. It could be other people. Instead of the Crisis Staffs, the commissioners would be active. It's not correct that a commissioner could replace the Crisis Staff. It was possible but it wasn't a rule that the commissioner would be automatically the president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the last sentence of the first paragraph, it reads: "Under the said decision, which is being sent to you, instead of the Crisis Staffs, War Presidencies shall be set up in the municipalities at a time of imminent threat of war or state of war." Sir, is it true that a state of imminent war had already been declared in the Republika Srpska on 15th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you agree that a declaration of imminent war had been made prior to your letter going out?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a long time since then, so right now, I really cannot put the dates together.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: All right. If we could have D446, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I move away from this document, perhaps I should tender 65 ter 16943.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 16943 receives number P6905, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, on our screens, we see a decision which reflects that an imminent threat of war is declared, and this is -- do you agree this is dated 15 April 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'm looking at you, is there any dispute about this date, the declaration of the imminent threat of war. Is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, as far as the Defence is concerned, Your Honour, the date and the document are not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, we're not here to teach the witness what apparently he does not know or doesn't know anymore, but, rather than to see whether he -- so therefore there's no dispute about this. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, sir, would you agree that after your 31 May 1992 letter regarding the decisions about the War Presidencies or the War Commissions, that that decision was superceded by a decision issued by President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision that I signed, the decision -- I didn't understand the question. Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir -- and perhaps I'll try to be less confusing. Thinking back to the letter that we just saw that you signed on the 31st of May --

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: -- is it true that that decision was superceded by another on the 10th of June, 1992 to set up War Presidencies?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presidencies are one thing, and the commissioners' offices are another. It's not the same thing, presidency and the commissioners' office.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, simply for continuity of the record without going down this alley too far, I'd place on the record that that decision is P4906, without going to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, we'll now go to a final direction - and we can take this off the screen - with respect to your statement D760, in paragraph 24, you claim that the party wanted to avoid bloodshed and that Nikola Koljevic went to see Tudjman and others in early 1992 to request he take all measures to prevent the Croatian conflict from spreading into Bosnia. If we could have P6727 on our screens. Sir, this is a transcript of a meeting between Koljevic and Tudjman and I'd like to ask you some questions about this in light of paragraph 24 of your statement. And we'll go to initially page 13 in English and page 17 in the B/C -- in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, we are all aware that the witness in paragraph 24 says what he was told at the time. He was not present during that meeting, so please keep that in mind when you ask him questions. Because to again, to tell the witness what was discussed at a meeting where he wasn't present and even if he has received information about that meeting which is different from what you think may have been said and where you have perhaps good reasons to think that is not what the Chamber -- what assists the Chamber in a great deal.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: All right. I'll quickly try to get through this area, Your Honour, and wrap this up.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir in the middle of page 17 in your -- in the original, we see Joseph Manolic on the Croatian side clarifying succinctly what Kojovic is saying. He asked: "The aim of that reorganisation would in fact be the homogeneity of certain areas." Koljevic replays: "Yes, the homogeneity of certain areas." Sir, Koljevic was actually in Croatia to discuss population exchange in Bosnia, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, according to my information, no. While preparing for Nikola Koljevic for that visit - Nikola Koljevic is now deceased - the main objective of all those who were present including him, was to do everything possible to stop the bloodshed and to prevent war from erupting. The war had already started. It was already raging in Croatia so the wish was to stop it spilling over into Bosnia. The goal was to seek all sorts of modalities to prevents that. One of those modalities would be also to discuss confederation. Not ethnic cleansing but ethnic homogenisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And in fact, sir, the ethnic homogenisation that you've just described isn't that, in fact -- well, let me restate this. In paragraph 26 of your Karadzic statement, D760, you say there can be no deportation without war and Serbs were persistently opposed to war. Sir, isn't it the truth that the goal was, in fact, to secure political, territorial and human separation of the Serbian people from others; right?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the general objective. The objective was in places where there were conflicts already or a potential for conflict to do everything to prevent bloodshed. That was the policy in the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bibles. Mr. Stojanovic, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few, Your Honour. Could we look at document P6905, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting, Mr. Witness, this is a letter, a circular letter. You have it in front of you. And the first thing that I would like you to tell the Court is the following. This letter is sent to three addresses and to files. What is this abbreviation SAO?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Independent autonomous region Herzegovina and then SAO Romanija and then SAO Semberija. That means independent autonomous region.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the reason is, why this letter was not sent to the municipal Crisis Staffs. Rather, to the three addresses mentioned here, the three autonomous regions?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I already said that it was very difficult. Communication already became difficult and the postal services were in a state of crisis as well so it was easier to reach these three centres and then through them, this could reach the municipal organs because these were regional organisations, in a way, so through them, this would reach the municipal organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, may I put one question for clarification. Mr. Komad, you were asked what the abbreviation SAO stands for. Your answer was independent autonomous region. Can you explain what the S stands for, the letter S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Samustalna, independent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Not Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I have a follow-up. What did the difference between independent and autonomous?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, yes, yes. Well, I mean, well, an autonomous region in a way is in conjunction with the central authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is not independent. But now what does -- what does independent mean in that context then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is less dependant on the central authority and -- and it depends more on central authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if it's autonomous it is somewhat dependant on the central authority. If it is independent, it is independent of that central authority. Isn't this a contradiction in terms in this name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there can be no contradiction if that is the way it is defined. If it is defined as an independent autonomous region. So that is to say, that, in a way, it is independent in certain aspects, but if it is autonomous then it is partly linked to the central authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We'll take it not further. That's your interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, of course, SAOs have been discussed quite a number of times in this court. Is there dispute about what the abbreviation, what the acronym stands for, between Prosecution and Defence? I'd like to know. Do you -- is it your position that it's independent or that it's the S stands for Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not discuss the topic with the Office of the Prosecutor. I think that we could agree on what this abbreviation stands for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that -- what -- if you think you would agree it's my impression, my provisional impression that the Prosecution think it is stands for Serbian. So if you think you would agree with the Prosecution, then that would mean that you also take the view that S -- the S in SAO stands for Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we're just going to take a look at these decisions that have to do with the time-frame in May 1992, and then, together with the OTP, we're going to try to stipulate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although I ask you for your position, but -- okay. Let's -- let's -- let's move on. Perhaps we ask the witness: Did the acronym SAO never stand for something there in which the S represented Serbian rather than independent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on the basis of my memory, as far as I can remember, it's the way I've already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you have no recollection that at any point in time, that SAO stood for Serbian autonomous region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say. I do not have that recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Komad, in this letter that you signed, there's a reference to War Commissioners in municipalities during an imminent threat of war or a state of war. Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether War Commissioners were there as appointed from the republican level, the central level?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The government of Republika Srpska appointed commissioners who were in charge of particular municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to end with another question related to this document. If you know, can you tell the Trial Chamber what the reason was, why in May, the end of May 1992, at the level of the Serb Democratic Party and the Executive Board, a decision is made to abolish Crisis Staffs and establish War Commissioners in municipalities?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just say that this decision was made by state organs. The SDS was the initiator and I mean, the initiator of such a decision. As for the reason that you're asking about, this is what it was. Precisely because of communication and co-operation that was greatly impeded, the assessment was that one would operate more functionally through War Commissioners than through Crisis Staffs; the Crisis Staffs that had existed until then. That was the reason why there was this move to this mode of operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now have document P6901 in e-court. Mr. Witness, this is one of the documents that you had the opportunity to see yesterday during the cross-examination. And now I'd just like to ask you to tell us when you focus on Article I of this decision, it says there that the territories of the municipalities, local communes and populated areas in which the plebiscite was held, when the Serbian and other peoples voted on whether they wanted to remain in the joint state of Yugoslavia together with the Republic of Serbia, the Republic of Montenegro, Krajina, Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and in which more than 50 per cent of the Serbian electorate voted for the same joint state. And then the sentence continues as follows: "... as well as those places in which other peoples and nationalities, ethnic communities, voted to remain in the same joint state of Yugoslavia shall be considered the Territorial Defence of the federal state of Yugoslavia." Please, what was the aim of this decision in relation to the area where citizens belonging to other ethnic communities voted in favour of remaining in the joint state?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The aim was in terms of the 50 years at least that people spent living together in the same state beforehand, the SDS had this objective or aim or orientation to stay in this joint state with other ethnic groups rather than have any kind of ethnic cleansing that was discussed here. So the SDS wanted other people who wished to live in this common state to go on living in this common state, this joint state.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the referendum?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Plebiscite, sorry, that was carried out on the 9th and 10th of November, whether there were such situations too. Namely, that areas where the majority population was non-Serb voted in favour of remaining in the joint state of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases; specifically in Sarajevo and in some other places too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you name those --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Truth to tell, not a major percentage was involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "not a major percentage was involved"? What do you mean exactly by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I mean, that already then there was this euphoria of the conflict and it was the Serb population that had mostly voted for the plebiscite. That's what I meant in terms of the largest percentage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But now the question was quite clear. You were asked about areas where the majority population was non-Serb voted in favour of remaining in the joint state of Yugoslavia. You said there were such cases. Could you name them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said: Tuzla, Sarajevo, Bijeljina. But not to a high degree or high percentage. I cannot remember the exact percentage points involved but I'm speaking in global, general terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say that you vote in favour of remaining in the joint state of Yugoslavia, that means that the majority votes in favour of that. That is, more than 50 per cent or if there are more choices, at least -- Could you -- Sarajevo, the whole of Sarajevo or certain municipalities of the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, some municipalities. Not the majority. Some of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Say, Novo Sarajevo. The municipality of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Novo Sarajevo, first of all, was there a majority of non-Serbs living there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was half/half. I cannot remember exactly. But it was half/half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is vital if you say that an area with a majority non-Serb population, then -- then to say, I don't know exactly what the number was and it was approximately half, that doesn't give a good example of what you are telling us. Because you are telling us where there was majority non-Serb population, that they voted in favour of staying within a federal Yugoslavia. Now, you say Novo Sarajevo. You don't know for sure whether there was a majority non-Serb population. Any other example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for example, Bijeljina. Bijeljina. In Bijeljina too. Although the Serb population was the majority population but there were also other ethnic communities there as well, specifically the Bosniak people. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you understand that are you contradicting yourself within two or three minutes. You were talking about an area with a majority non-Serb population. I ask you for an example, you say Bijeljina although there was a majority Serb population. So it is not an example of what you were telling us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Specifically, Ilidza. That's where the population was Bosniak, the majority population. And there was a large percentage that was in favour of this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they vote in favour of? That is, did the majority vote in favour of staying within the federal Yugoslavia, or, as you told us now, there was at least quite a number of non-Serbs who were voting in -- to remain in the former Yugoslavia. So what -- what we need is a majority non-Serb population. You say that's Ilidza. And then we need them to vote in favour of staying in the former Yugoslavia. Did the outcome of the Ilidza vote, or plebiscite, was that by majority, they wanted to stay in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, specifically, I cannot remember about the exact percentage. But, I mean, well, as for this question of yours, well, the majority was where the Serb population was, I mean, where the majority population was Serb. That is where the majority voted for such decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not the -- the problem. That's not the issue I raised with you. Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us - if you know - what the reason was and motive for the adoption of the conclusion of the Serb -- Assembly of the Serb People in Bosnia-Herzegovina in October 1991 on the need to have a plebiscite and a vote for remaining in the joint state of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina faced major test because as Yugoslavia disintegrated, the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina were supposed to become a minority people and they were outvoted in different forms of political activity and a coalition was created between -- I mean, the Croat leadership and the Bosniak leadership. And in that situation, the Serb people remained a minority. So all decisions that were made by the organs of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was outvoting there so the Serb people and the Serb leadership I mean, saw clearly that there would be this kind of outvoting, and that they would be ignored and that was one of the basic reasons, I mean, for the Serb leadership to adopt this kind of decision because in practice in political activity, there are many examples that can be mentioned, especially in terms of how the then-Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina operated as well as other organs where the Serbs were being outvoted and where their voice could not be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I shall conclude by dealing with just one topic. Can you remember whether the ballots that were used during the plebiscite was there only one form or colour that was used or were there several forms, several contents, several colours?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKA KOMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same form and the same question was on all the ballots, however for technical reasons, I think there were two colours for sure and maybe even three. The yellow and the blue, as far as I can remember. So there wasn't any different content involved. The content was the same and the form was the same. However, there were two colours. I think there were only two. For technical reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness explain what the technical reasons were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, printing presses couldn't, for example, they couldn't give us enough in the same colour. And then we opted for, say, sending the yellow ones out in order to check this better, certain regions so that we'd see where they came from. Yellow, blue, it didn't really matter. It wasn't that they were particularly determined in any way. It was for technical reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that simplest is to make them all white or -- is it documented anywhere that it purely had to do with technical matters rather than perhaps make a distinction between to whom they were distributed? Was there any way that the different colours were distributed in a different way in an area where the vote took place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I've already said, this was just a technical reason. There was nothing else. I mean, I don't know what you mean, what your association is. However, as far as I know, this was just technical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You earlier told us, I think, that the various ethnicities voted in a similar or a different way. You said Serbs voted this way; other peoples voted not the same as the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received the information from the field, and we were informed that people were coming. We didn't have the precise data so I couldn't give answers to your previous questions because of that. We didn't count people along religious or ethnic lines. For example, we would receive a report from Bijeljina and then the people who conducted that would tell us that there were many Bosniaks or perhaps a lot of Croats who had come to vote, depending on the area. We don't know how people voted but we knew what the turnout was. There were commissions that monitored the plebiscite and this was something that was set by the assembly, not by the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The different colours in the ballot papers played no role whatsoever in either the way in which the vote took place, neither in the interpretation of the results of the vote. It was just ignored because it was only for technical reasons. Is that how we have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for this assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, on behalf of Ratko Mladic's Defence team, I would like to thank you for answering the questions that we put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Any further questions, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes. And in light of this last area, there will be about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have to take the break first. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we'll take a break and there will be a few more questions for you after the break. And we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Stojanovic, you heard the evidence of the witness about the different colours, purely technical, and about questions being exactly the same, no differences at all. Of course, we've spent quite some time on it. Is it -- does the Defence want to rely on that evidence given by this witness, that it's purely technical? Because under those circumstances, it makes sense, I take it, that Ms. Bibles wants to show the ballot papers and that the questions are not exactly phrased the same and that there is a link between a colour and the -- do you want to rely on the evidence of this witness in this respect? Because then we would go through the exercise again, I take it. If you say, Well, I'll not rely on that because that's not the Defence's position, then we can perhaps skip the matter and -- of course, there's -- it still sheds some light on the reliability of the evidence of this witness but that's, of course -- that will not change in this way if we go through that evidence, the ballot papers. What's your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we're not going to rely on that part of the witness statement. The questions were directed at a different area, so that's why I stopped. So we're not going to be dealing with that part of the witness testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You mean you -- you accept that there was a difference and that the colours are not just for technical purposes? That there were different questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we would like to have the witness into the courtroom. But, Ms. Bibles, I can imagine you would not need the full ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could clear up one additional thing it might be helpful. Over the break, I spoke with Mr. Stojanovic and I believe we are in a position to stipulate SAO does -- the parties concur it does mean Serbian autonomous region. I just want to confirm that on the record before we go forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there's a stipulation that that's the meaning of the word "SAO". But apart from that, do you have any further questions of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In light of the Defence position with respect to the ballot, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll ask the witness to come in and -- I think it would be fair to the witness to tell him that there are no further questions because the parties agree that it was not of a purely technical nature and that the questions were not exactly the same but since you agree, there's no need to ask further questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In the meantime we can take care of a quick housekeeping matter from yesterday and that was 65 ter 20251 which was MFI'd under P06902, pending provision of the audio CDs. Those CDs have now been provided to the Court Officer. So P6902 can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections from what I understand. P6902 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, perhaps to your surprise there are no further questions for you, and I'd like to briefly inform you about what happened in your absence. The Prosecution and the Defence agreed on SAO to mean Serbian autonomous region. That's one. Second, the Prosecution and the Defence agree that the different colours in the ballot papers were not just for technical reasons. And, second, that the questions as formulated on the ballot papers were not exactly the same, and, therefore, since the parties agree on this, there is not need to further elaborate in detail with you on what exactly the questions were or what colours there were. Under those circumstances, the questions -- the parties have no further questions for you. Neither has the Bench. Which means that this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Usher, could you escort the next witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. MacDonald will be cross-examining the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there was ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you have not responded in any way to what Mr. Traldi said about the list and the ethnicity of the persons. If you would wish to do so, of course, you'll always be given an opportunity but you didn't stand up when Mr. Traldi spoke. Or after Mr. Traldi spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it's Mr. Stojanovic's witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, do you want to add anything to what Mr. Traldi said?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, Your Honour. I would like to thank my colleague Mr. Traldi for what he has just said. I don't have anything to add. I don't have any problem with that. And I stand by the suggestion that the document be tendered into evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We don't object. As to the ethnicities, we stand by the position I provided this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, any number with the document? I think it was mainly a matter of interpreting the document, names on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no P number. Neither a D number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was 1D1733. Is that correct -- 2733. So it was not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm very reluctant to quibble about punctuation in the transcript but at page 27, line 18 I -- it changes the meaning of what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that we deal with the matter not now immediately because the witness is waiting and it's not very polite. Mr. Sipovac, it's not very polite when you enter the courtroom not to address you in the first place. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Sipovac. Mr. Sipovac, you will first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You find him to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll first kindly ask help from the usher to distribute statement summaries to the translation booths and type recorder, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sipovac, please excuse me, I was just dealing with some administrative matters. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Good morning. And it could already be good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, the Englishmen say good morning until noon.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: In our part of the world, it's different. It's already good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I sent an e-mail that I would kindly ask for extension of time for my direct for one hour and 15 minutes. I hope I will not uses all the time I'm asking for, but I have to do some corrections that are already made in Karadzic trial and I have to go through all of them and one more so we will have more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, a lot of the time allotted to you are spent and all these corrections than really to have hear the evidence. If we have to do it, of course, we can't have anything in evidence which is not accurate. So -- but it's better done before we come to court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's Karadzic statement and corrections were made on Karadzic transcript. So we have to do the same corrections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you can take a new statement and then make those corrections. But let's leave it to that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we have 1D2514 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it's a good habit to start to ask the witness to -- to identify himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Sipovac, you heard His Honour. Could you please tell us your first and last name slowly for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: My name is Cedo Sipovac. I was born on 19th of April, 1959 in the municipality of Nevesinje. If you need any more information about me, I can continue. Is -- is that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. That is sufficient. Did you provide a statement to the Defence team of Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we please look at the last page of the document that we're seeing on the screen. On the left-hand side is the B/C/S version of the document. Do you see the document? Do you see the signature? Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: It's the 18th of January, 2014. And then, to the right, it's my signature. Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now look at paragraph 3 of your statement. In the B/C/S version, that is the first page. In the English version also it's the first page. In the paragraph, it says that sometime in June 1991 pursuant to an order from the Secretariat of National Defence, military territorial districts were formed. In your testimony in the Karadzic case, you corrected this, and you also drew my attention to it. You told me that these military territorial districts actually were manned at the time and that they had been formed before; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: The decision to form them was earlier in early 1991 and they were manned in late 1991 in July, August, September. This applies specifically to Prijedor. So there is a difference between forming them and actually staffing or manning them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So instead of having "were formed," we should have "were filled with personnel" in this part of paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two other corrections in this paragraph. We need to look at the next page in both versions of the statement. The -- the numbers of military posts are wrong so that the numbers in the last sentence, 3673, should correctly read 3670. And number 7672 should correctly read 7362. Mr. Sipovac, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 10 also there is a correction. It's the previous page in the B/C/S and English -- ah, ah, now we have both pages on the screen. The first sentence states: "I cannot recall the exact date in 1992," it should state: "I cannot recall the exact date in 1991 ..." Sir, is that correct, Mr. Sipovac?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. In paragraph 10, that is the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now we just need to look at paragraph 1. From the time that Mr. Sipovac testified in the Karadzic case, he changed jobs, and in that version of the statement, it says the following. I'm going to read the whole sentence in English. It's the last sentence but one in this paragraph [In English] I quote: "I'm now [Realtime transcript read in error "not"] an official in the veterans organisation of Republika Srpska in Banja Luka." And this sentence in paragraph 1 should read now: "I am now an official in the Ministry of Labour, War Veterans and Disability Protection." [Interpretation] Is it correct what is stated here?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: The interpretation was that I'm a functionary, an official. Fortunately, I am not a politician. I'm not a functionary. That word in Serbian would designate an official. But I am actually just an employee. And so I don't want to leave the wrong impression. And also if that is of any importance here, I have four grandchildren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lukic, I'll not comment on the last -- the importance of the last part of the witness's statement, although I think in view of the age of the Bench, we have some understanding for it to be important. But it's -- looks as if on page 31, line 24, that there was a Freudian mistake. I think you read I am now an official and not I am not an official although that forecasts already that he is not anymore a -- an official. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sipovac, after making these corrections, is the information in your statement accurate and truthful?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would like it tender Mr. Sipovac's statement into evidence, as well as the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] There is no associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you want to tender no associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want to inform you that there is no associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection against the ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: There is no objection, Your Honours but I think one more correction has to be made, a typographical error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's really purely typographical and creates no confusion we'll do that. You will inform the Chamber after you have consulted with Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm obliged Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is purely typographical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It changes the meaning of the [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it's not purely a typo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: In the last page in the English, Your Honours, and I believe it's the second-last page in the B/C/S, English under attachment C it states: "I have described everything I know about facilities of imprisonment in question number 16," and I think given the renumbering of the paragraphs that should be question number 15, Your Honours, on the previous page in the English. Aside from that, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not just a typographical error. That affects the content. Witness, could you read what appears under attachment C. And at this moment you see on your screen that there's no question 16 but there is one number 15. Was it your intention to refer to your answer to question 15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you permit me to read I mean, I think it's obvious that there is no question 16. But, still, I would like to be permitted just to read it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would just read your answer to question 15 and then tell us whether you do -- did or did not want to refer to that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then we have to go back one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But only in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did give that answer, that I wouldn't change my statement and I stand by that even though my opinion is different. It doesn't matter if it's called a camp or something else. The important thing is what was going on there. But I do leave it at what is written here. If that's the whole point of the question that you are putting to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you say the names are without importance. Whether that's true or not is another matter but we leave that to the parties to argue. But your reference was to your answer to question 15. Madam Registrar, the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2514 receives number D766, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will first read statement summary from Mr. Sipovac and I'll have several questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cedo Sipovac was an official in the Secretariat for People's Defence in Prijedor. He will testify about the situation in his municipality, before and after the first multi-party elections. Cedo Sipovac will testify about the mobilisation process in the municipality of Prijedor. He will testify that all members of the war units were called up, and conscripts received same type of weaponry, regardless of their ethnicity. He will testify about the instruction that was sent from Jerko Doko, then republican secretary of national Defence in B and H. Mr. Sipovac learned from his colleagues that in his instruction, Mr. Doko banned the secretariats from mobilising war units. Mr. Sipovac testifies that he did not have any information, nor did he receive any instructions or orders, ordering the permanent removal of Bosnian Muslims and Croats from Prijedor municipality, nor he participated in anything of that kind. Mr. Sipovac claims that if this had been the policy of the authorities, the defence structures would have known about it. Cedo Sipovac will testify that sometime in June 1991, military territorial districts were replenished and the responsibilities of the secretariat were shifted, that is to say, the tasks of recruitment, the mobilisation of TO war units. In accordance with this order, one such organ was formed in Prijedor municipality with its centre at the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks. That was the short statement summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please put the question you had in mind to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sipovac, you told us that you worked on mobilisation tasks. After the conflict broke out in the area of Prijedor, were there any military conscripts, Croats or Muslims, in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm specifically going to ask you about what you know about the ethnic composition of the Ljubija Battalion.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: The Ljubija Battalion, the 6th Motorised Battalion, was manned by people from a multi-ethnic area and the makeup included Serbs, Croats, Muslims, I think also ethnic minorities, Ukrainians. So it was a homogenous [as interpreted] unit. I don't know what else I could say. It was carrying out its assignments in line with the commands of the -- orders of the superior command and within the unit, as far as I know, there were no interethnic disagreements or conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How were the units manned? What was the principle involved? Ethnic, territorial? Tell us what the principle was.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: In view of the circumstances that affected the records and the process of mobilisation, at that moment, the most efficient way of manning units was the territorial principle, which would translate as follows. You mentioned the Ljubija Battalion now and it was manned from the territory of several local communes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please pre-trial the names of the communes distinctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You really have to speak distinctly, so that people could hear you, understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Especially the local communes. Could you please repeat the names of those.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. So the Ljubija Battalion was manned from the territory of the following municipalities: Miska Glava, Donja Ljubija, Gornja Ljubija, Surkevac, Ravska, Ljeskare, Cikote. Now have I forgotten someone? I don't know. But that would be it. In some of these places, both Serbs and Croats lived, and Muslims. The other battalion, Omarska Battalion, it was called, it was manned from Omarska, Gornja Jelicka, Donja Jelicka, Maricka, part of Petrov Gaj, Lamovita. If necessary, I can enumerate the others, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: That was the territorial principle and it depended on the ethnic structure of the population that lived in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have just a percentage of -- what percentage was Serb, what percentage was Muslim, what percentage was Croat in that battalion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now I'd have to give a free estimate, Your Honour, if that's acceptable. The Ljubicki battalion, I cannot give you the exact percentage but it certainly had over 100 persons who were of a different ethnicity and also some of the commanders were ethnic Croats. I think that we can speak at the level of the entire war-time unit and say that there was 10 per cent or even more. If we look at the brigade in total in this battalion certainly had up to 25 percent. Perhaps even 30 per cent. I'm speaking about the Ljubija battalion. It depends. Perhaps 80 per cent was Serb, ethnic Serbs because that was the structure of the population in that area, that the 3rd Battalion was also multi-ethnic. It covered part of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... witness, you've answered my question about the Ljubija Battalion. You said it was -- up to some 80 per cent was Serb. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be around that figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know roughly in this Ljubija battalion what were the losses, in terms of ethnicity, provisional figures?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say in terms of battalions but I know this thank there were Muslims and Croats who fell victim. It's a bit difficult to comment upon this but I think 37, 38 persons who were non-Serbs were killed, if we look at the level of the entire brigade. The Ljubija battalion, of course, it's very difficult to speak about the victims and certainly one cannot speak flippantly of these figures. Persons who fell victim, but I think it was about ten persons. I think that we can find these statistics somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they receive different assignments, members of different ethnicities, who were members of that unit?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's say the Ljubija battalion. Did Serbs get different tasks from Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, the commanders of the unit were who they were but certainly there were never any objections and I don't think that anyone ever gave separate tasks to Muslims, separate to Serbs, separate to Croats. That kind of thing did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know it or do you think it? I mean, if you have any knowledge. Mr. Lukic, you know how important it is for this Chamber to know about facts rather than impressions or opinions. Do you have any specific knowledge about it, please tell us. If not, then we will be able to understand your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I don't have any specific knowledge about any orders being issued on ethnic grounds in the unit, any kind of tasks on such grounds. That is to say, that all were given totally equal treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you say, I have -- I don't have any specific knowledge about any orders being issued on ethnic grounds, do you have any knowledge on orders not to be issued on ethnic grounds or -- which means that would you have to know about orders. Have you seen orders? Do you -- are you familiar with orders issued within that battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not take part directly in commanding that unit. But I claim this because the principle of control and command from the top level was never such and, I mean, I haven't seen a document to that effect. I cannot say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Lukic, what, in principle, I mean, facts, that's what the Chamber is trying to find out. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do, can I ask for clarification of the previous answer here. Mr. Sipovac, at page 38, lines 22 -- he says it's a bit difficult to comment upon this, but I think 37, 38 persons who were non-Serbs were killed. And then later at line 25 or 24 you say persons who fell victim but I think it was about ten persons. I'm not quite sure what the ten persons represent. I know the 38 represent non-Serbs. Who are the ten persons who -- who fell? And how did they -- how do you reconcile them with 38?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first figure I stated, as I did all this work, as I co-operated with the veterans' organisation well, my knowledge is based on the brigade level. Out of the total number of casualties, persons who were members of the brigade who were killed, a brigade is larger than a battalion. Thirty-seven, 38 persons who were non-Serbs were killed. Within the battalion itself, the Ljubija battalion, it was about ten people or ten people. But that can be checked. The exact figured can be checked in the records. I mean, the differences in the level, a battalion is a lower-ranking unit than a brigade. Perhaps that is the best way in which I can translate this for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. So 38 died in the brigade; ten died in the battalion. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipovac, since you manned units, do you know whether all members of a single units was sent, for example, to the corridor? Irrespective of ethnic background, were they given the same tasks?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: The unit is an organisational unit would get tasks as a unit and there weren't any special tasks or orders that were based on ethnic background; Serbs, Croats, Muslims. That is to say, when an order is issued the order is issued according to the principles upon which it should be based. It depends on what was involved. That would not be right. It would not be based on the rules. It would not be humane. It would just be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you something about paragraph 8 of your statement, and I'm going to ask you to explain something related to the mobilisation problems faced. In 1991, the beginning of 1992, were there problems with call-up papers?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: 1991, 1992? Did I understand you correctly. Sorry, what was that that you said? End of 1991, beginning of 1992, well, there were problems in carrying out mobilisation absolutely. Both in 1991 and in 1992. Because different instructions arrived in terms of how mobilisation should be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: The signal for mobilisation goes along parallel lines, that is to say, down the structures of socio-political communities, political organs, down to local communes. And then there is control and command. That is to say, the military chain down to the war-time units. Should I repeat all of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There's no need to do that. Just a minute, please. Just stop. You spoke about the system in your statement. When I'm asking you about problems, mobilisation problems, perhaps my question was not phrased very correctly. Were there any problems on the ground? Persons who were on the ground, who were distributing call-up papers, did they face problems?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. And there was a problem involved in the mobilisation procedure as such and that's what I wanted to tell you about. Because the leaders, the political leaders of the Muslim Bosniak people that is, or rather persons who headed the organs of the Croat people too, for example, the secretariat, the Republican Secretariat for National Defence, they gave instructions to ethnic Bosniaks and Croats not to respond to call up or, rather, that organs should not mobilise war-time units of the JNA and then this was followed by what happened on the ground. The couriers faced problems, those who were carrying call-up papers. I can't remember the exact name but in 1991 I remember that one of these couriers was killed. This was a Bosniak in Sanski Most, and then also in Prijedor, in Cejreci that is to say, the couriers who would carry call-up papers they would be stopped by people, for example, I remember this special case. This person who had an automatic rifle told him that he would be killed if he continued distributing call-up papers and there were other problems too. There were quite a few problems, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from the details is there any dispute between the parties that mobilisation in that point in time there was problems and hesitation by non-Serbs to follow the call-up? I'm not talking about details. And I'm also not talking about what means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or what consequences it may have had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I wonder if I can check and come back to you with that question, just with regard to the time-frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, of course, I meant it to see whether we could shorten the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a question to the witness. I hear what the whole detail that he has given which doesn't seem to correspond with what he says in paragraph 8 of his statement. Paragraph 8 of his statement states that both -- all ethnicities responded to the call-up. And then, of course, the last sentence says: The Muslim and Serbian response continued to be very poor. Doesn't seem to refer to any specific ethnic group alone not responding. So this is new in relation to paragraph 8. And I'd like to find out which is which between the two.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both are correct if I understood the question as it was interpreted to me. Mr. Lukic asked me where were some problems and I said what the problems were. I did not say that there was no response but did I say that the obstruction calls were public. I can give you an example if you want a specific example. Although I'm not -- well, I'm going to tell you, for the sake of the truth to help you, to help us all. I personally received the following task: For security reasons, nobody wanted to go to Kozarac, Kozarusa, Kamicani, Trnopolje, because there were incidents there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Could you slowly repeat the names of those local communes.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Kozarac, Kozarusa, Kamicani, Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Only Kozarac has been transcribed. You see how you have been speaking.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Stop now. Next?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Kozarusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Kamicani.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, this was one of the routes taken by the couriers. The centre was in Kozarac. Now what does this mean? That is to say, that that is where one comes with the mobilisation signal and with the call-up papers for that area and then the couriers take the call-up papers and ask the messengers to come in and then they personally hand over these call-up papers to the conscripts. In January 1992, on orders received from the superior officer since no one, none of the instructors, that is, none of the couriers wanted to carry out this assignment, I as the desk officer, took this upon myself, and I distributed, I think about 1400 call-up papers, if I remember correctly. I took that to Kozarac. The person that I found there that is responsible for carrying out mobilisation was a person who was new to me. This was not a person who had been registered with us. He did not want to accept this task or its implementation and he said that he would not guarantee my safety and security irrespective of what I was supposed to do. I asked him to give a statement to that effect. He didn't want to. I compiled an Official Note on account of that. And I returned to the command post and I informed the superior officer about the contents of my Official Note. So I don't want to accuse anyone, but this is a route where, it just so happens it's a question of coincidence. This is where the population was primarily Muslim. Muslim. Ethnic Muslims. So that is a specific case, if that is what we are discussing. I'm not saying, and I cannot challenge anything -- I mean, it's not that I'm challenging anything. I would like to confirm that there were a number of persons of Muslim ethnicity, Croat ethnicity and others that were in the Motorised Brigade. Some of them came in September 1991. Others came later. Others left the unit on their own. Others went on work obligation at the request of the work organisations where they were employed. So there was no distinction whatsoever. Their rights did not differ from the rights exercised by ethnic Serbs. Perhaps I've spoken a bit too extensively but I hope I've explained this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's just mentally return to Cejreci. You said at the cross-roads in Cejreci that a person with an automatic rifle threatened another man who was carrying the summonses for -- to be delivered. Do you recall the names and can you tell us the ethnicity of the person who was delivering the summons and the one who made the threats?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Gredelj was the last name of the person. And the other one was Amir Ramic. Gredelj was the one making the threats, whereas Amir Ramic - I think that was his first name - was the person who was delivering the summonses. They were both Bosniaks, I'm sure of that, because I was doing that work and I had the files in front of me and all the records. Then Mr. Ramic no longer wanted to take part in this whole system because he was the victim of threats. This was sometime in January 1992, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Once the call-up began and people started to go to the Croatian front, were people leaving their units, there were any problems with the units where Serbian people were members?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: You mean when they started to go to the front?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The question relates to the period when the first conflicts broke out in the north of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sijekovac.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: What is characteristic is that the mobilisation of units from the Prijedor area, people from there were replenishing 37 different units. A large number of those units were mobilised in 1991, and the response was the way I described it. The events in 1992, as a consequence, had the following. At one point in time - I think that was in April or May, maybe even June of 1992 - there was a large concentration of military conscripts who had returned from the front. They left the units on their own once they found out what was happening in their municipality, let's say the municipality of Prijedor. I'm emphasizing Prijedor, in particular, because after the attack on Prijedor, after the events in Dobrovoljacka Ulica, after the attack on the Tuzla column, there was a large concentration of people who had come back but had not placed themselves at the disposal of the war combat units. They were out of the system. They had not returned their weapons. And this created a lot of problems for me. I was working on the mobilisation. Their assignments, war-time assignments were different, in a different place. The civilian police was used to try to resolve this matter. There were also killings in -- in restaurants where people from the same ethnic groups would kill each other. So roughly speaking about the return, there were always individuals who ran away from the units. Serb, Croats, Muslims. But if we're talking about something that was of significance -- influence, that -- then that would be those who were returning from the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it's a break time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is. Could you tell us where we are in terms of time, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll probably need another 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please keep in mind that the more important the matter is, the more we are interested in details. The more marginal the matter is, the less we need details. Witness, we'll take a break, and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sipovac, may we continue?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at the statement of Kerim Mesanovic in e-court. It's P3414 now. [In English] This is attestation. We'll need probably the fourth page. And English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I do not know what your questions will be, but usually I take it that you're familiar with the procedure that you first ask the witness about the substance and only then put statements of other witnesses to him. Again, I do not know what your questions will be and will be covered by what you already asked him.
