utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sipovac, did you know Mr. Mesanovic, Kasim?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Kerim, not Kasim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Kerim. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1991, was there ever a situation where orders relating to the mobilisation were mostly issued by Serbs? And could you please tell us who was at the head of the Secretariat of National Defence and who was head of the mobilisation section?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: The chief of the mobilisation sector was Dzevad Habibovic in 1991. And the chief or actually the secretary of the secretariat was Becir Mendunjanin. As for whether the Serbs were the ones who were issuing the mobilisation orders, it's not a personal thing. Anybody could sign it. It could be a Serb, a Bosniak, a Croat, but the organ, the actual body is the one that issues an execution order for mobilisation, it could be the commander of the war unit or anybody else. It goes from higher ranking to lower ranking unit. There could be the secretary for national Defence. So it's not a personal thing. It's not a question of whether they were Serbs. It's not something that happens because a Serb or a Muslim issues an order. It's a matter for the organ. Perhaps by their action or non-action --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, now you have three times told us the same. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you notice at that time what was the ethnicity of Mr. Mendunjanin, first of all, and Mr. Habibovic?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: According to my information and in view of the facts that I was keeping the records, according to my information, therefore, they were Muslims. And this is also something that Mesanovic said in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask the witness how you know what Mr. Mesanovic told in his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had the documents during preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In that situation, when the organ was headed by a Muslim and when the mobilisation section head was a Muslim, in that situation, did you notice that it was the Serbs that were mostly issuing the mobilisation orders?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in paragraph 7 of the statement of Mr. Mesanovic you can find this claim although he confirmed that on -- those two names heading those two departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the head of the republican organ who was the person there, do you remember, and of what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Of the Republican Secretariat?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: It was Jerko Doko. And he was a Croat. I didn't have his dossier in my hands in order to know but according to the distribution of functions, he was a member of the Croat ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mobilisation orders, did they began to arrive from Belgrade bypassing the authorities in Banja Luka and Sarajevo at any point?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: The orderings were arriving from Belgrade in any event because the seat of the secretariat was there. So it was normal that the orders would be initiated from that place. You said bypassing Sarajevo and Banja Luka? I don't think that they did, because if they were in the position or I was in the position of seeing my colleagues who were carrying out the mobilisation duties, say, that they received a document from the Secretariat for National Defence that was headquartered in Sarajevo and they were acting pursuant to that orders, it means that Sarajevo was not bypassed, Banja Luka was not bypassed either, because the Military District Command or the administration of the military command was headquartered in Banja Luka, so we received our military order through the Military District Command. So I don't believe that they were bypassed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The assertion that they were bypassed is also something that is referred to in paragraph 7 of Mr. Mesanovic's statement. Meaning Banja Luka and Sarajevo were bypassed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... page 3, actually two pages ahead from this point. This claim is on the next page, in paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you head the military territorial organ in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was at the head of the military territorial organ in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: It was Major Milivoje Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 8 of Mr. Mesanovic's statement says that Mr. Sipovac headed the VTO. Were there any non-Serbs who were employed at the VTO?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give us a name.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Semso. Right now I cannot remember his last name. Semso was his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was he the only one, or what was the number of non-Serbs employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he was the only one. It's not that that is what I think. That's for sure, actually. He was the only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how many people were employed in the VTO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At first, there were four, five -- eight. Eight. Eight of us all together. I'm sorry. I'm sorry I have been speaking this way. But it was not more than seven or eight, but I had to go through all the names. In Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem. And you said at first -- yes, eight was the highest number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well I can count them, actually. I would have to go through all the names, but I don't think that there's more than eight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know Mr. Muhamed Burazovic?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've already spoken about Dzevad Habibovic and Mr. Mesanovic.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they also join the VTO?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The people who were transferred to the VTO, were they supposed to go through a security check?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I had to get security clearance and others probably had to as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who carried out these security checks for you at the time and for Mr. Mesanovic; do you know?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I know who ran my check. The security organ. I don't know if it's appropriate to give the name now, but if necessary, I can give the name too. Kresimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you want to us go in private session if it's easier for you to say then?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I've already uttered his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Mr. Habibovic recommended me and then I was interviewed. And then I know that Kresimir again, I cannot remember his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Kresimir's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Through the records that I kept, Kresimir was a Croat name. I knew that through the military records that I kept and files, so the gentleman is a Croat, I assume, but I cannot say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 9, we have comments in this regard. Mr. Mesanovic. Captain Radmilo Zeljaja, was he appointed to the department for organisation and mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 11, there is a comment in the opposite direction. That's what Mr. Mesanovic said. In the Autumn of 1991, did Captain Zeljaja come to take over the entire database from the mobilisation department?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you present when somebody came?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. There was Lieutenant Zoran Ristic, the personnel officer in the 343rd Infantry Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 12 of Mr. Mesanovic's statement, we have content that is directly opposite to this. Do you know what the reason was for taking this documentation out?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: When military territorial organs were established, secretariats of National Defence were duty-bound on the basis of the protocol and the order of the Federal Secretariat to hand over documents that had to do with recruitment and mobilisation. This was not made available to us. They did not allow us to take this over, and that is why the system of mobilisation was impeded as well as the system of recording military transcripts. Specifically, this unit was fully manned from Prijedor and -- and therefore we did not have proper records at the time. Military records. That was the only reason. According to the law, they were duty-bound to hand over the files.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know Mr. Radmilo Zeljaja?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge was Mr. Zeljaja a member of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: That I don't know. I found his name in certain documents that I read. I really am not sure. Whether he was, whether he wasn't, I think he attended some sessions, but I don't think he was a member. As far as I can remember, when I testified in Dr. Karadzic's case, I found this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Thank you. Mr. Dzevad Habibovic. What do you know about his employment from 1991?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Dzevad was head of the Department for Mobilisation and Recruitment. Now what I know about his employment is that he was chief at one point in time. I think that when I was transferred to the military territorial organ, I think that a Croat came to this position. October 1991. Because of this political distribution of posts. I think Gotvald Joze was the name of the Croat who replaced Dzevad. Because according to this division of the structure of power in Prijedor, the Croats were given this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So what happened to Mr. Habibovic, his work, his job?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I don't know. According to the law, he was given a job, if that was possible; otherwise, he was unemployed. What else? Since he was an official, a functionary. As far as I know, he did not have a particular post. He was not assigned to a particular position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when this status of his started in terms of not being assigned to a particular post and how long that lasted?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I am not aware of the details. I think it was September 1991. Now, since these are administration organs usually it was six months. It was for six months that a person could enjoy such a status. So it's possible that it went on for six months that he was not assigned to any particular position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If someone is not given a particular job within those six months, what happens to such a person then?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to remember right now but I think that according to the law, then this person becomes unemployed. If such a person meets retirement requirements then such a person can retire or otherwise this person is unemployed or an attempt is made to find him a job elsewhere in the administration, in view of his education, personal experience, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But this job that he left when he received this status of being a person without a particular assignment or position, did he lose that job?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, of course, he lost it. If I understand your question correctly, of course, he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What time-frame are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's from 1st of October, 1992, until 1st of April -- 1991 was the first one until 1st of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who headed this organ? Who gave him this status of a person who was not assigned a particular position?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: It is the secretary of the secretariat that had the right to regulate the status of an employee in that way, and I think that it was Becir Mendunjanin who was head of the secretariat then. He certainly was. It was certainly Becir Mendunjanin in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where is Mr. Dzevad Habibovic today?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, we'd see each other in Prijedor and just recently I received greetings from him indirectly. He told someone to say hello to me. But otherwise I would see him in Prijedor. He is in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this now: Did you ever hear that on the 4th of May, 1992, there was an incident on the road between Prijedor and Dubica in which all the Muslims who happened to be on a bus were killed?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I saw that as I was reading documents, and I think that in Dr. Karadzic's case I was asked about this. I don't know. I tried to ask around, but I did not hear of such an incident. I personally don't know. I don't know what happened, when it happened. I have no personal knowledge about any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P3415, could we briefly take a look at that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a decision, as you can see for yourself, dated the 4th of May, 1992 sent to the Secretariat for National Defence. And it says here: "Pursuant to a decision of the Ministry of National Defence of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, dated the 16th of April, 1992, the government of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina hereby adopts the following decision: 1. We hereby order general public mobilisation on the whole territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." At the time were you aware of this document? Did this document reach you?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge that you were supposed to act on the basis of this document?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 1, did it actually pertain to the work that you did?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Since it's mobilisation, it does have to do with the work that I did. But none of all of this that is down here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Now let me ask you this: Did you go with Mr. Kerim Mesanovic to Zitopromet with a hard disk that contained mobilisation data. Can you tell us what happened and why you went there, if you did?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did go. I don't want do repeat what I've already said. I stated that military department did not have any of the records that we needed because the secretariat would not give us any of these files, and the electronic files were kept at the Secretariat for National Defence, and then I mean, it was Mr. Mesanovic, Kerim Mesanovic, who was in charge of the electronic data and I did go with him and they were saying already in 1991 that something was wrong with the system. I'm not very knowledgeable about this. And they said that this didn't function with this basic whatever it was, that this did not work, the diskette did not work and everything else. And then we went there -- well, it was along those lines and then all of a sudden there was this possibility, because we went every day. Well, not every day but we went several times to ask for these records in order to be able to carry out our tasks. We even talked to Mr. Mendunjanin. That is to say, the chief went, the assistant Chief, I went and a few other colleagues and they always invoked the council for the national defence of the municipality of Prijedor that did not allow us at the military department to use the existing military records and files and that's the way it was. I don't even remember if we asked for it or whether they invited us but I'm sure that I went with Mr. Mesanovic and I cannot remember who else went with us. We went to Zitopromet because the system did not function properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you announced another 20 minutes, approximately. Well, you are far beyond that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sipovac, did you issue an order to Mr. Mesanovic that he should mobilise people only of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: First of all, I was not Mr. Mesanovic's superior so I couldn't issue assignments to him. He could only have received assignments from his secretary or the chief. I don't know who he got this one from. To issue an assignment to only ethnic Serbs, did you say? I don't remember. But had I done that, perhaps I did it because in the previous period we tried several times to send more summonses to all three groups. But I don't recall telling him that, and in my concept of thinking, it's not something that I would say to him. If I said that, I wouldn't consider it a mistake because I worked for everyone, including Serbs, Croats and Muslims. So perhaps if I did issue that order or tell him to do that, maybe that was something that needed to be done at that particular moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are many words for a simple answer that you may have, you may not have, you don't remember exactly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And can you just tell me this: After the conflict broke out, did the Serb authorities forcibly mobilise Croats and Muslims and did they forcibly mobilise Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: There was no forcible mobilisation of anyone. There were regular summons, as far as circumstances permitted. There was no force applied towards Serbs, Croats, or Muslims in terms of their legal duty to respond to the summons. So I believe that what Mr. Mesanovic said had no relation to -- or did not correspond to what was actually happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sipovac. Those were all my questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic, you'll understand that such a last answer that -- where the witness refers to what Mr. Mesanovic said, that we've got no idea what he is talking about. We know we have a statement of Mr. Mesanovic in evidence but what specifically he is referring to, the Chamber doesn't know and you [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... if I can draw your attention to paragraph 16 of Mr. Mesanovic's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's your answer. You are now giving testimony. I do understand that you think that the witness may have referred to what Mr. Mesanovic said in paragraph 16. That is ... Mr. MacDonald are you ready to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sipovac, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. MacDonald. You find him to your right. Mr. MacDonald is counsel for the Prosecution. And may I urge you to answer questions in a focussed way rather than very broad, going to all margins of the subject, that are perhaps covered by the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: And the best of fortune to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, you told the Court where Mr. Habibovic is just now. Can you tell us the Court where Mr. Mendunjanin is just now.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I found out during the trial of President Karadzic that Mendunjanin was unfortunately killed in the Omarska camp. Before that, I wasn't aware of that. But we were in exceptionally good relations. But since the Presiding Judge said I should not speak to -- in too much detail, I will stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And did you know that Mr. Mendunjanin's wife was also held in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: You asked me if I knew if his wife had been detained. Actually, I didn't know that Mr. Mendunjanin was captured and detained and even less his wife. During my testimony in the Karadzic case, I got this information. I was asked if I knew that he had been exhumed. I said that I would only speak the truth here, and I am speaking the truth. Up until time I didn't know about it, and I'm sorry that it turned out like that. This was a man whose conduct towards me was extremely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The simple answer is that you don't know. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic was also arrested and taken and held in Omarska camp, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I saw that he was there from reading his statement. I saw from the statement that he had given to the Prosecution that he was in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Perhaps I can turn to your statement now, Witness, which is D00766. I'm looking for paragraph 14, which I believe is page 7 in the English and page 5 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I seek one clarification. In your statement, you said that there were no camps in Omarska, just an investigation centre. By confirming that Mr. Mesanovic was arrested and taken and held in Omarska camp, you said: "I saw that he was there from reading the statement ..." Does this include that you agree there was a camp in Omarska or is it still your position that there was an investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when the witness -- no, I'm sorry, when the lawyer was reading my statement and at the intervention here on paragraph 18 and the answer, and so on, well, would you please permit me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Would you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my opinion, and according to the information that I had, it was an investigation centre. But the least important thing is what we will call it. What is important is what was going on there, and I said that already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it was important enough for you to say in your statement that there was no camp but an investigation centre. So apparently you yourself pay some attention to words used. But you say, according to your information, still, it's an investigation centre and not a camp. Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm going to summarise paragraph 14 of your statement, Witness. You were asked whether the police at CSB or SJB level were involved in a list of crimes which include murder and deportation of Bosnian Muslims or Croats from the territories of Bosnia-Herzegovina to which the Serbs laid claim. Your answer is that you did not know about such an involvement and had that been the policy of the authorities, the defence structures would have known about it. What do you mean by the phrase "defence structures"?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I was speaking this at the time all of this was happening, saying that I didn't have information. Later there were, of course, stories and I had to find out because I lived there. Defence structures, what I meant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the whole introduction. Please answer the question, rather than making these kind of introductions. What you did mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was what are the defence structures, is that correct? Structures of -- of All People's Defence, military and civilian structures. Civilian structures socio-political, communes, all the way down to the local communes. And the military structures --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you slow down as well. The interpreters are unable to follow you. Could you please resume from where you said: "Civilian structure, socio-political, communes, all the way down to the local communes." And then you continued: "And the military structures ..." and could you resume from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The system of All People's Defence, I said, we have the system of all socio-political communities from the federal republican down to the local communes. All socio-political organisations that function at the time made up the system. Then, the units of the armed forces made up the system. The units of the civilian protection. Also the units responsible for monitoring and alarm, and then all the other structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: That's a long list of bodies that make up the defence structures. You're not claiming, are you -- and I would appreciate a short answer to this. You're not claiming that you knew everything the defence structures knew, are you?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: In view of the job that I was doing, I had to know the basic principles, of, let's say, the defence policy and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: My question: Did you know everything the defence structures knew, all knowledge. Are you saying you knew that?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I did not know everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: And I couldn't have known everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to your personal knowledge now. You're aware that a massacre was committed at Koricanske Stijene by the SJB in August of 1992, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: When did you find out about that massacre?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Please believe me when I say that I don't know. I had the same question. I really don't know when I learned about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Don't tell us what we are -- you want us to believe. Tell us -- you say you don't know when you found out about that massacre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't remember when I found out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you find out before you gave the statement? That is, in 2014.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did, yes, I did. I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you -- you -- why -- so you know at least a little bit about when you gained knowledge about that massacre. Could you tell us if you know that you knew it earlier than - what was it, January 2014? - then to say I don't know anything about it is not the full answer. Did you know it during the war? Did you know it after the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the war, definitely, 100 per cent. I'm really speaking this sincerely that was not part of my work, so I found out about it after the war. Definitely not during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But how could know that. If you say I don't know when I learned it, how could you say it was after 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know by my own reactions. Because I would have to bring up some personal things here and some feelings. But I know definitely that it was not during the war, and since I lived in a mixed marriage, I'm speaking about personal things. My wife's name was Fatima, and I know that is a kind of measure of correction in my life, so I know. I definitely did not know it during the war. Even the duties that I was carrying out did not require me to know about that. If we can finish with this, that would be good, but if it's something that needs more clarification, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you tell us you don't know when you learned about it. But upon further questioning, it turns out that you knew it before 2014 and that you did not know it until 1995, so there must be more to be said about it when approximately you would have heard. Because if you don't remember, you can't say that it was not during the war or that it was not after 2014.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You put a question to me, if I remember when. When you put the question, whether I remember whether it was before or after the war, that's an answer I can give. I can tell whether it was in 1997, 1998, 2000 or immediately after the war, yes, but I really don't know. This is something that I didn't know. I really didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'm telling you why that was. I told you why that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, you've told the Court that you found out prior to giving your statement to the Karadzic team, so when you answered that question and said you did not know about the involvement of the police, in particular, with regard to the murder, extermination and deportation of Bosnian Muslims and Croats, that wasn't entirely accurate, was it?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, that's my information and I said I didn't know. I don't know who committed that. I didn't know then. If you established in court proceedings if that this was something that was committed by policemen, then let it be so. I'm not by nature such a man to ask around or to talk or to find things out. So I really don't know. Now you're telling me it was the police. I didn't know. I have no reason to lie. Had I known who it was why wouldn't I have been of help to assist in resolving the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Do you believe the defence structures, as you have laid them out, would have known about this massacre?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would object here. Because my learned friend already established that he didn't know what defence structures knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is denied. There is a good reason to put this question to the witness. And, Mr. MacDonald, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Sipovac, I asked you if you believed the defence structures, as you have laid them out, would have known about this massacre.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I didn't know at that point in time, if we're talking about then, I didn't know. And now when I'm reading, this was the last time I saw, then I saw that it was the police. So now I have the information. If I have understood the question. I'm not trying to evade an answer. But I see it's the SJB forces, if they did that, then, of course, if that was so, it's natural that they would have known about it. If I understand my question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sipovac, you did understand. My apologies. Yes, Mr. Sipovac, you did understand my question correctly. The reason I asked is that in your statement and you answer to this question, you state, had this been the policy of the authorities the defence structures would have known about it. Now do you accept that these things did happen, that the defence structures did, in fact, know about them or you don't know, rather, if the defence structures knew about them?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Now you are putting the question to me in relation to things that I didn't know, but it's based on my statement and information that I had at that time. Now it's a question of whether it was the public security centre. I don't know if this was done with or without the knowledge of the structures of politicians. I don't know. Somebody should have been in the system who would have known that, whether they were from the political or other ranks, if this was an organised or a planned thing, somebody would have known about it. So now I really cannot puzzle out what it is that you would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, paragraph 14 is -- and that, of course, is one of the problems, gives conclusions of the witness and I think you have established that he -- well, at least he says I didn't know anything about it. So the conclusions are just as bad as his knowledge. Mr. Lukic, of course you have to consider this as well, that if you present statements in which, I could say sweeping statements if you see what the witness did not know about it could be, he did not know anything and then to say if it would be different from what I did not know, then others would have known about it. That's conclusion. That's a kind of logic which doesn't assist the Chamber. Mr. MacDonald, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I will move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, you spoke today about the 6th Battalion. I'd just like to ask you a couple of questions on that topic. Was that part of the 43rd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The 43rd Brigade was part of the VRS, the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the 6th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: His name was Rade. Rade ... my mind is blocked. We called him Cica. He was later replaced by Misa Ostojic [as interpreted]. Right now my mind is blank. I cannot recall his name. His nickname was Cica. His first name was Rade, later he was replaced by Misa Stojnic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness can I suggest that his name was Rade Bilbija?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Of course, yes, why not? Bilbija yes, that's right. It was Bilbija, yes, nickname, Cica. Yes, I just couldn't remember right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I look to move to a new topic, but I look at the time. Perhaps we should take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could take a break. Could you please try to -- to give a time-frame to the last answer. Because the witness said initially it was and then -- so could you please seek to clarify that and then we'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: When was Rade Bilbija commander of the 6th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: When it was just formed. I think in 1992. I cannot remember exactly. And then 1994. I'm not sure about this information. I mean, it's just roughly but he was there at the beginning when the battalion was formed and then until 1994. I'm not sure, though I think that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That being clarified, Witness, we'll take a break again. We'd like to see you back at 25 minutes to 2.00. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, would you give us an indication as where we are in terms of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I hope to finish in 25 to 30 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which would still mean today. I don't know whether you have a lot of questions, Mr. Lukic. We could try to see whether we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not so far. Maybe one or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One or two. Then there's a fair chance that if everyone makes a good effort that we would be able to conclude the testimony of this witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, I'd now like to move on to the topic of mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have P02871.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: While this is brought up, can I tell you these are the minutes of the fourth meeting of the Council for National Defence of the Prijedor municipality on 15th of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: P02871, Your Honour. If I can ask for the top of page 2 in the English whilst we remain on the bottom of page 1 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The transcript doesn't mention the name of the -- of the organisation whose meeting this is. Maybe you want to place it on record. This is the National Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It is the Council for National Defence of the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, you reported to that council on the topic of mobilisation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, there couldn't have been any other reason for me to attend that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: We see that Vladimir Arsic also contributed to that discussion. He was the commander of the 343rd Motorised Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: No, no. You got that wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it yes, or is it no, that Vladimir Arsic was the commander of the 343rd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard 342nd in the interpretation, and that's why I said no. And then when they said 343rd, then I said yes. So it was misinterpretation and then the interpreter apologised, so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The 343rd Motorised Brigade of the JNA became the 43rd Brigade of the VRS; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: We also see Vladimir Zeljaja participating in this discussion. He was the deputy commander of the 343rd Motorised Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: No, not Vladimir Zeljaja. Radmilo Zeljaja, correction. But yes, he was deputy chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction. If we could move to the second page of the B/C/S but would remain on the same page in the English and I'd like to draw your attention to point 4 after the words, "The following conclusions were adopted." It states: "In the assignment of the remaining conscripts to units, priority is to be given to the reenforcement of war units 4777 and 8316." Witness, 4777 was the 343rd Motorised Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution now please have P03032.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness this is a one-page document in the B/C/S. It is a 2nd Military District order for mobilisation and it is dated the 12th of May, 1992 and type signed by Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: We will need the second page in the English.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I see that it's the 2nd -- I see up here command of the 2nd Military District, the 11th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wait -- wait for a question to be put.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention to point 3 which is for Your Honours at the top of the page which states: "When recruiting, give priority to: Motorised and artillery units, armoured mechanised units, military police units, reconnaissance units and units for anti-armour combat. I'd like to ask if this order from the 12th of May was discussed at your discussion on mobilisation on the 15th of May, three days later?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this document and this is the first time I hear of this. Quite frankly, I'm telling you, so, this is the first time I hear of this. I really don't know about this. So this is the first time I hear of this, this is the first time I see this document and this was not discussed as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Witness. Do you recall if war unit 4777 was then given priority by you and your colleagues in assignment of the remaining recruits after your discussion on mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I don't recall the actual proceedings of the session. Now why priority was given to these units, they were Prijedor brigade. 4777, by establishment, was one that had priority in terms of manning. However, the percentage was not satisfactory. It went on in 1991, continued in 1992, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question was whether in fact was, given the decision to give priority for the assignment of the remaining recruits as we saw it on this minutes, was it done or was it not done? That's the simple way of asking it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know on the basis of what document. I received orders from the command of the Military District. I did not receive orders from the municipality or anybody else or, rather, it was the military department that received this. Now what was acted upon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, please try to answer the questions. We saw a document in which it was stated what units would receive priority in recruitment. Was that done or was it not done? If you don't know, tell us. If you do know, tell us whether it was or whether it was not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have P00151.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And, Witness, I'd like to have page 2 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S. Perhaps I should say this is a 1st Krajina Corps report to the Main Staff of the VRS on the 31st of May, 1992. Witness, you spoke about problems in terms of mobilisation. If I can take you to the bottom section the B/C/S, it's point 5, number B state of morale. And a few sentences in, we see the words "after the actions in Kozarac ..." Can you find that sentence, sir?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: The part where it says Kozarac, Sanski Most. Is that what you are referring to? That some conscripts of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... you asked me whether I see it. And I was trying to ask you whether that's the sentence that you mean. So is that that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Sipovac, that is the sentence I mean. I'm right in saying it reads: "After the actions in Kozarac, Kljuc and Sanski Most, some conscripts of Muslim nationality have asked to be released from the units. They express their dissatisfaction with the massive destruction of their towns." Do you know, sir, if this negatively affected mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, it certainly affected mobilisation in a negative way because people were leaving the unit. However, I believe it would be interesting for you to look at the whole document. If you allow me to explain, I can provide an explanation. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wait for the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sipovac, I'm actually going to move away from this document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have P03841.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, this is an interview with Radmilo Zeljaja, where he discusses the 43rd Brigade. The appreciate the B/C/S is quite small. If we can move to page 2 in both -- both languages. And if we can zoom in on the B/C/S and the most left hand column, this is the part in bold towards the bottom left. Yes, thank you. Witness, you see the words in bold there in the Cyrillic. Am I right saying that interviewer states --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What part are we looking at in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour. The middle paragraph the first bold line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: At one time, you said that such structure of the brigade suited you. I'm just asking you, sir, not to read it out but do you see that part?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot understand what the witness is saying. Could he please be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean this part. The policy of the SDA, the SDS, the HDZ. Is that the part that you want me to read? I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'm going to read it out and then I'm going to ask you a question about it. In the English it states the name "Radmilo Zeljaja" and then: "We soldiers think that the policy of the HDZ and SDA suited us because if the Muslims and Croats had responded to the mobilisation, we would have had two brigades. One would be ours and one Muslim-Croatian." Now, sir, do you recall if the attitude expressed by Zeljaja in this article was similar to anything he said at the discussion on mobilisation in May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: I don't know which statement of mine you mean. Do you mean what I said here now or something that I said earlier on? Could you explain that question of yours. I did not understand what you meant. Which statement of mine?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Sipovac, we have established Radmilo Zeljaja contributed to the discussion on mobilisation in May of 1992, the meeting that you were at. Here we have a statement of Radmilo Zeljaja made about mobilisation in late 1991. Do you recall if the sentiment he expresses here, that it suits certainly him and he says soldiers that Muslims did not respond, if he made any similar statement at the meeting, in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think it would be only fair to read the next sentence and then ask the question or about the sentiments or facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can do so in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But without that, it's -- I think, at this moment [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... not a correct presentation of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll leave it -- I'll not force you to do it, Mr. MacDonald. If you think, I have no idea what Mr. MacDonald is heading for, and certainly there was an opportunity to deal with the matter in re-examination. But I take it the witness has read it anyhow by now so, therefore, so you please, Mr. MacDonald, either repeat your question or rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Sipovac, I'm happy for you to read on in that -- in that paragraph. But for the purposes of this question, I'm asking whether you remember if Radmilo Zeljaja ever expressed a sentiment that it suited him and soldiers that Muslims and Croats did not respond to this mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: No, no I don't remember that. Really. I don't remember that being discussed at the session of the council. I really don't remember. However since I know Radmilo Zeljaja, I know him personally. This really has nothing to do with his sentiments. It has do with his idea to be a soldier -- I mean, if this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you've answered the question: No, you don't remember that. That's an answer to the question. All the rest was something that was not asked. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If we turn to page 3 in the English but remain on the second page in the B/C/S and if we could scroll just slightly to the right in the B/C/S. And the part in the English is at the top, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, the last bold section in that second column the part that is now in front of you, it concerns the SDA becoming increasingly aggressive and the JNA being an obstacle in its way. In Radmilo Zeljaja's answer he states the brigades command was immediately linked to the SDS giving them important support, as they do for all decent Serbs, to organise themselves for self-defence in case of attack by the Muslim forces." Were you aware of JNA units supporting the SDS at this time?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'd like to discuss one more part of this document and the B/C/S I believe it starts on page 1 and continues into page 2 and it is all on page 3 of the English. I believe in the B/C/S it is the third column towards the column. I think the one just underneath the picture. Witness, can I ask you to look for the words - and you don't need to read them out, just let me know when you find them: "We knew that from that the days of mobilisation onwards ..."

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, we knew that part. Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and for Your Honours, it is the second paragraph on the page towards the end of Zeljaja's answer about four lines back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, it reads: "We knew that from the day of mobilisation onwards, we would lead the people we took into battle until the very end and fight for the goals that are fighting for now. We have never given up these goals, and this is the creation of a Serbian state in these areas." Were you aware, Witness, from the day of mobilisation onwards that Radmilo Zeljaja was planning to fight for the creation of a Serbian state?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'd now like to move to my final topic, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: This is on the replacement of personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: On 30th April 1992, Slavko Budimir became secretary of the Secretariat of National Defence in the Prijedor municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Are you asking me? I didn't quite understand. Is this a question for me. Yes, yes, I didn't understand this comment. Slavko Budimir replaced Becir Mendunjanin as secretary of the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And Slavko Budimir is of Serb ethnicity; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, you were in the VTO until August 1992.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Were you aware of the dismissal of officers on the basis they were Muslims and Croats at any time in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: In the Army of Republika Srpska? To the unit that I was in? I don't remember anyone being dismissed on account of them being an ethnic Muslim or Croat. They could have been dismissed only if they did not carry out orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, in the answer you limit the scope of the question to the unit that you were in. The question was broader, however, and covered the VRS in its entirety. Would that change your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have insight into such documentation and I cannot give any comment. That means that I stand by what I know. Namely, that in the 43rd Prijedor Motorised Brigade on the basis of ethnic affiliations no one was dismissed, rather, only on the basis of not carrying out orders and then they could have been resigned to a different post or something like that. I really cannot give you any comment with regard to other units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because you don't know or because you haven't seen documentation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my answer would be unfair it I were to say I don't know. That means I don't know because I have not seen any documentation. I mean, I cannot give comments on something that I haven't seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I sometimes do know things although I have not seen documentation. That's my question. Are you aware of any Muslims and Croats being -- being fired or in one of the other units, apart from yours, on the basis of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Perhaps can I shortcut this topic just to --

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: In war-time units. In war-time units. I have no such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whatever units. We're talking about the VRS. Does that change your answer in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would not change my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have P03753.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: This document is titled: Conclusions adopted at subregional meeting of political representatives. These representatives represent a number of municipalities, including Prijedor. It is dated the 7th of June, 1992. If we can turn to page 2 in the B/C/S but stay on page one in the English and it is point 4 to which I'd like to draw your attention. Witness, here we see the first line that reads: "We demand that the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka, and particularly General Momir Talic of the 1st Krajina Corps, purge the 1st Krajina Corps of Muslims and Croats." Witness, the 43rd Brigade was part of the 1st Krajina Corps. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution now have P03892.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And this is a report from the 1st Krajina Corps to the VRS Main Staff and the Serb Republic Presidency. It is dated 9th of June, 1992, two days after the document we just saw. If I take you to the main paragraph, which reads: "It was stated ... within the units of the 1st Krajina Corps, 14th PoB and the units of the RV and PVO in Banja Luka garrison there are 67 officers of Muslim or Croatian nationality. An ultimatum was issued requesting removal of these persons from vital and command posts by 15 June 1992, or they will take over control over the OS. We consider their demand to be justified, but it is impossible to find adequate professional replacements among the reserve staff, and active officers of BH origin are not arriving from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." Witness, were you aware that the 1st Krajina Corps command considered a demand to purge these staff identified as Muslim or Croatian nationality as justified?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Witness, just before we move away from this document, I'd like you to note that the operational confidential number is 488-3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution now have P03893.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And this, Witness, is an order from Ratko Mladic to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. You can see that there is a reference to document strictly confidential number 488-3 of 9 June 1992. This document from Ratko Mladic is also dated 9 June 1992, and the body of the text reads: "Officers of Muslim or Croat [sic] nationality must be sent on leave immediately." So, Witness, within the 1st Krajina Corps, do you accept there was an intention to remove Muslim and Croat officers on the basis of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: When I read this report, I get a different picture, and I think in the field there was a different situation. Many people refused to carry out their assignments and voiced their wish to be transferred to a different unit. I had a case where a Croatian officer asked to be transferred and this was approved. I don't know then and if this is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You disagree, that is clear. That apparently is your answer. You have a different opinion. You have the opinion you stated before. So, therefore, you've answered the question by stating that you disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: This will be my final question, Mr. Sipovac. Can the Prosecution please have P00217. Now, witness, you stated there may be a distinction between units in the field. This is a regular combat report sent to the VRS Main Staff. It is being sent on 13 June 1992. I need to move to page 2 in the English and page 5 in the B/C/S, and I'm looking at point 6 entitled: State of combat morale. Now the first line states: "The morale of the troops and units is basically stable. Contributing to this are the following ..." There is then a list of things but around five lines in in the English, we see a line that starts: "The purging of officers ..." Don't read it out, please, witness, but just let me know that you've found it. A simple yes will do.

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I found it where it says the purging of officers on an ethnic basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. And that sentence reads: "The purging of officers on an ethnic basis remains a topic of discussion because of the danger that it may very soon result in deficiencies in the units, but it is proceeding in the spirit of the order received." So my final question to you, Mr. Sipovac, is whether you now change your position and accept there was an intention and an effort to purge the 1st Krajina Corps of Muslim and Croat officers?

utterances.speaker: CEDO SIPOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, we are at 18 minutes past 2.00. I don't know whether the situation changed since you gave us your last estimate of how much time you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It did. And how much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 20, 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes so we can't do that today. That's clear. Mr. Sipovac I'd like -- we adjourn for the day, and we need a little bit of time tomorrow morning to conclude your testimony. Before we adjourn, however, I would like do instruct that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in whatever way about your testimony, whether that is testimony you have given today, or whether that is testimony you're about to give tomorrow. If that's clear to you, you may follow the usher and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30, although not in this same courtroom but in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn for the day and, again, thanks to all those assisting us, even though it's only five minutes and my reputation sometimes makes it even worse, but for staying with us for the minutes after quarter past 2.00. We adjourn for the day and resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 12th of November, at 9.30 in the morning, in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 12th of November, 2014, at 9.30 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.20 p.m.,
